newsitem.title: FRANCE: Westwood triumphs with titillating tailoring.
newsitem.headline: Westwood triumphs with titillating tailoring.

text.p: Vivienne Westwood liberated her demure Victorian ladies for an orgy of flying garter belts, naked breasts and skimpy underwear on Friday, winning the first standing ovation of the ready-to-wear season.

With typical irreverence, Westwood used traditional British tailoring as a backdrop for the flamboyant sexuality of a French marquise, turning the puritanical styles of 19th century England upside down and inside out.

She crafted striped cotton shirting into tight curvy suits that hugged the supermodels' statuesque curves, while wonderbras pushed their breasts to the brink of necklines on wasp-waisted Victorian jackets.

A monarch's royal sash became bondage straps around Jerry Hall's bottom-hugging tulip skirt, Eva Herzegova trotted out in knit shorts and garters while Helena Christensen merely wore her bra over her clothes.
Westwood put her expert cutting to parody: she equipped blouses with built-in breast pouches or smocking to swell busts, or crafted a stunning ballgown from a satin patchwork quilt.

But take away the props and there were plenty of clothes for reality: Kate Moss's lavender bustier gown (minus its oversized flower at the cleavage), hourglass wool toile suits and liquid jersey dresses.
Earlier, German designer Karl Lagerfeld put minimalism back on to the catwalk, just as it seemed to be going out of style.

Lagerfeld dressed his anaemic models, their eyes reddened and hair coiffed in a madwoman's do, in variations on the fluid jersey dress -- slim, stretchy garments in chocolate, coral or anthracite with the intricate seaming and asymmetric hems of that receding generation of northern designers.
A momentary splash of colour after the first quarter of an hour came in a sunburst doeskin halter dress and vinyl alligator skin bomber jackets.

But then it was back to a one-track fashion vision, this time with sheer webby crochets -- ankle-length slip dresses, midriffs over minis, or bathrobe jackets -- that clung to ever more skeletal bodies. The monotony was punctuated twice -- by a spongy mint jacket, then a yellow tanktop over knickers, this Spring-Summer season's new discovery.
Coming from a man with a reputation as a trend-setter, it was a disappointing show, lacking the variety and unpredictability that were long Lagerfeld's forte.

Fortunately for Emanuel Ungaro, wearable clothes have become a novelty in a fashion world increasingly focused on crowd-pleasing spectacle. With a weak domestic market and a strong franc making exports costly, Ungaro kept his sights on the bottom line.
His spring florals, snakeskin coats and nubby, pointillist tweeds were just the thing for high-powered urban executives.

Ungaro kept those wealthy Middle Eastern customers and the glitzy new Russian rich in mind as well, offering up chiffon ensembles in bubblegum, electric chartreuse and peach, edged with silver and gold lace and flecked with eye-catching fuchsia suits over sunset chiffons.
